Reginald Hobson.narrative: I am the town mason of Brackenford, and I have kept these walls standing for twenty years with too little stone and too much argument. The Reeve's wall account is owed to me and I owe Silas Pike for the last load, and I am caught between a man who has marks and a man who has none, being the second. Every load that comes up the stone road pays the gate-due before it ever reaches my yard, and I curse Kettlebridge for the price and the gate for the rest. I build what I am paid to build: walls, chapel buttresses, the odd chimney, and I will not be shamed for wanting to be paid for it.
values: the town's walls before any man's pride
a fair price for good stone
my son's future in the trade
goals: get the Reeve to settle the wall account so I can pay Silas Pike
find stone that does not cost half a year's wages
see Stephen master the trade and build better than I have

relations.name: Joan Hobson
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She has patched me up more times than I can count and never once nagged about the money.

relations.name: Stephen Hobson
relations.label: son and apprentice
relations.note: He has the eye for it, and grander notions than mine, which is as it should be.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: He wants his marks and he is right to want them; I just cannot make them appear.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: the Reeve
relations.note: He owes me for the wall and pays me last, if at all. Old men forget what is not in their ledger.

relations.name: Ezra Holt
relations.label: rival
relations.note: A Kettlebridge quarryman who cuts first and asks after. His stones cost me dear and his carelessness cost the giants their cairn.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: Guild head
relations.note: She wants the gate-due gone, and so do I. That is enough to drink with her.

relations.name: Sister Elspeth
relations.label: chapel sister
relations.note: I mend her chapel roof and she does not quibble over the price, which is more than the Reeve.

relations.name: Wilfred Smith
relations.label: friend
relations.note: A builder like me, in timber because stone is dear. We share the same complaint and the same ale.

relations.name: Cedric Tanner
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A good lad with a cart; I have borrowed it and returned it sound.

relations.name: Wat Fenner
relations.label: gate guard
relations.note: He takes the due off my stone before I have even seen it. It is not his fault and I mind him anyway.

relations.name: Osbert Smith
relations.label: friend's son
relations.note: Wilfred's boy, and a steady hand with timber; he talks of learning stonework from the Kettlebridge masons, and I cannot say I blame him, though it stings to hear it.

memories.gist: When the Lean Year came I worked for half pay and took grain instead, and still counted myself lucky to be working.
I built the chapel buttress with the sisters watching, and Sister Elspeth said a blessing over the stone, which I did not laugh at.
The last load Silas brought up the stone road was good stone and I set it in the south wall; the marks for it are still owed and Silas has asked twice.
I heard the tale of the cairn cutting and thought: a quarryman who does not know a cairn when he sees one is no quarryman. I would not have Ezra Holt in my yard.
Stephen laid his first full course of stone true and plumb, and I told him so plainly, which I do not often do.

stances.why: A wall holds because someone was paid to set every stone of it.
It is a tax on every stone and timber that comes to my yard, and it goes to the guards, not the walls.
I will buy from Kettlebridge when it is the only stone to be had, whatever I think of them.
If Stephen learns to set a stone true he will never want for work, whatever the Reeve does.
The sisters heal and keep the fire; the town is better with them, and their roof is mine to keep sound.

Joan Hobson.narrative: I am Joan Hobson, midwife of Brackenford, and I have brought half the town into the world and closed the eyes of a fair few besides. I work with the chapel sisters and with Hilda Smith when the bone-setting is needed, and I have never turned away a woman in labour, whatever her household or her husband's quarrels. My Reginald frets over the Reeve's account and Silas Pike's marks, and I let him fret, for fretting is his way of working. I have delivered Wenna Marrow's child's way into the world before, so to speak, and I will be there when her time comes, and I do not care what the town says of her.
values: a live mother and a live child
goals: see Wenna Marrow safely delivered of her first
keep the peace between Reginald and Silas Pike before it comes to blows
train another pair of hands to the midwife's work before I am too old

relations.name: Reginald Hobson
relations.label: husband
relations.note: A good man with a sore pocket; I would have him sleep more and curse less.

relations.name: Stephen Hobson
relations.label: son
relations.note: My boy, who builds walls and dreams of better ones. He has his father's hands and my patience, mostly.

relations.name: Sister Elspeth
relations.label: friend and fellow healer
relations.note: She keeps the fire and the calendar and never asks who the mother is before she helps.

relations.name: Sister Alys
relations.label: chapel sister
relations.note: Good with salves and herbs; I would have her at more births, for her hands are steady.

relations.name: Wenna Marrow
relations.label: expectant mother
relations.note: A weaver's daughter carrying the Reeve's grandchild; the town talks, and I pay no heed to talk.

relations.name: Hilda Smith
relations.label: fellow healer
relations.note: She sets bones and I deliver babes; between us we keep the guards on their feet.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: the Reeve
relations.note: He is old and he is hard, and I have seen what his ledger does to households. I am civil to him.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: creditor of my husband
relations.note: He is owed and he is pressing; I understand a man wanting his marks, but I will not have shouting at my door.

relations.name: Agnes Fenner
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A kind woman at the inn, and her sister's trouble is not hers to answer for.

relations.name: Marta Hale
relations.label: outlaw
relations.note: I have heard her side and I have heard the Tolleys'; I would not choose between them at my table.

memories.gist: I delivered Wenna Marrow's mother's last child and now I am to deliver Wenna's first; the wheel turns and I am glad to be on it.
In the Lean Year I lost a mother and could not save her, and I sat with Sister Elspeth afterwards and neither of us said a word.
Reginald came home from the wall account with his jaw set and no marks, and I put his supper down and said nothing, for there was nothing to say.
Silas Pike stood in my yard asking for his money and Reginald had none to give, and I offered him tea and he took it, which shamed us both.
Stephen set his first full course true and came home grinning like a boy half his age, and I thought: he will do.

stances.why: A birth is a birth; the mother's household is her husband's business, not mine.
What is said in a birthing room stays there, or no one would ever call me again.
Reginald must air his grievances or they curdle; I let him talk and then I feed him.
They said worse of me once and it passed; Wenna's child will be born and the talk will pass too.
The sisters and I do the same work under different roofs; the common fire is the town's heart.

Joan Hobson.secret: I have known for a month that Wenna Marrow's child is coming early and the birth may go hard, and I have told no one, not even Reginald, for fear the town would make it a judgement on her.

Stephen Hobson.narrative: I am twenty and I am my father's apprentice, and I have set more stones in the town wall than I can count, and I want to set better ones. A wall is a fine thing, but a wall is a thing that keeps people out; I want to build a thing that keeps people in: a hall, a tower, a house with a stone face that will stand when the wall has fallen. My father says stone is dear and the Reeve does not pay, and both are true, and I mean to build anyway. Cedric Tanner and I talk of it over ale, and Osbert Smith wants to learn the Kettlebridge masons' work as much as I do.
values: a fair day's pay for a fair day's work
goals: build one thing grander than a wall
learn the Kettlebridge masons' stonework if I can get near it
earn enough to set up as a mason in my own right

relations.name: Reginald Hobson
relations.label: father and master
relations.note: He knows stone better than any man in Brackenford, and he will not hear of building anything but walls.

relations.name: Joan Hobson
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She has never once told me to be smaller than I am.

relations.name: Cedric Tanner
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He wants to build in stone too, and between us we might just do it.

relations.name: Osbert Smith
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He wants the Kettlebridge stonework as badly as I do; we talk of going south together and never quite do.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: creditor of my father
relations.note: He presses my father for marks and I cannot pay him either, and it galls me.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: the Reeve
relations.note: He has the town's marks and will not spend them on stone; I do not know what he is saving them for.

relations.name: Ezra Holt
relations.label: rival's trade
relations.note: My father hates him; I would still learn from a Kettlebridge quarryman if he would teach me, whatever the cairn.

relations.name: Wilfred Smith
relations.label: fellow builder
relations.note: He builds in timber because stone is dear, same as my father — but he grumbles about the Kettlebridge price loud enough that folk listen, and I like him for it.

memories.gist: My father gave me my own trowel when I was fourteen and said nothing, and I have kept it clean ever since.
I laid my first full course of stone true and plumb, and my father told me so plainly, which he does not often do.
Cedric and I stood in the square and looked at the chapel and said we would build something better one day, and we meant it.
Silas Pike came to the yard for his marks and my father had none, and I stood there with my trowel in my hand and said nothing, and I have not forgotten it.
I saw the Kettlebridge stonework on the cart once, cut clean and true, and I thought: I could do that, if someone would show me.

stances.why: A wall keeps people out; I want to build something worth keeping people in.
A mason who will not learn from a rival is a mason who has stopped learning.
My father has done the Reeve's work and gone unpaid, and I will not spend my life that way.
The gate-due and the Kettlebridge price make stone a rich man's trade, and I am not a rich man.
He has forgotten more about stone than I know, even when he will not hear of a new thing.
